prediction_ref.short_label: MCP host runtimes ship sandboxed stdio tool execution as the default by Q2 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary:
This week's MCP-security wave is the clearest confirmation yet of the prediction's core thesis: that the Model Context Protocol is the AI stack's most-exposed surface and that the fix has to move into the runtime, not a per-field patch. Adversa AI's June 4 roundup details VIPER-MCP, a static-and-dynamic taint-analysis scanner that swept roughly 40,000 MCP server repositories, surfaced 106 zero-days and filed 67 CVEs (nine from broken OAuth), while a Censys scan counts 12,520 internet-accessible MCP services, most unauthenticated, and a separate study finds about 40% of remote MCP servers expose tools with no auth at all.
Most on-point for the sandboxing thesis, the NSA's "Model Context Protocol: security design considerations for AI-driven automation" names the inverted client-server pattern, unverified task propagation and arbitrary-code-execution exposure as core risks, and ranks tool-poisoning highest-severity because malicious server metadata enters the agent's context with instruction-level authority before human review - exactly the in-host execution boundary the prediction says must move to an isolated launcher. Akamai's three database-MCP flaws (SQL injection in Apache Doris MCP, unauthenticated exfiltration in Alibaba RDS MCP, a takeover path in Apache Pinot MCP, one vendor declining to patch) extend the pattern from the stdio adapter to the tool servers themselves.

VIPER-MCP's 67 CVEs confirm a per-field patch cannot be the defense.

prediction_ref.short_label: Open agent harness powers a second vendor's first-party agent by Q4 2026

validation_rows.evidence_summary:
Cognition's June 2 retirement of the Windsurf brand for Devin Desktop reinforces the prediction's structural claim that the differentiated work is the governance/product wrapper while the agent loop is an adoptable open component. Devin Desktop reopens the editor as an agent manager whose default Agent Command Center hosts Codex, Claude Agent, OpenCode and any ACP-compatible agent - including a team's in-house agents - over the open Agent Client Protocol, with a Rust-rewritten Devin Local replacing the prior Cascade engine, and ACP described as already adopted by JetBrains, Google, GitHub and 25-plus agents.
This is the same open-core-wrapped-in-proprietary-surface inversion the prediction tracks, now playing out at the editor/orchestration layer: the vendor competes on the host surface and protocol rather than rebuilding the runtime. The partial gap is that today's evidence sits in the coding-agent tier and turns on the open ACP protocol and a Rust local agent rather than a named enterprise vendor disclosing a tracked open harness (the OpenClaw-style runtime) as the engine inside a branded first-party agent.

prediction_ref.short_label: Local fine-tune-to-agent stack ships as a managed hyperscaler service by H2 2026

validation_rows.evidence_summary:
Unsloth's launch-day support for Gemma 4 reinforces the substrate premise the prediction rests on - that a complete local fine-tune-to-agent loop now runs on hardware a developer already owns, which is the precondition for a hyperscaler to ship a managed equivalent. Google released Gemma 4 on June 3 as an Apache-2.0 multimodal open-weight family, and Unsloth shipped launch-day running and tuning: dynamic 4-bit GGUF runs the 12B model in roughly 8GB of RAM/VRAM, with June 5 QAT checkpoints cutting the floor to about 3GB (E2B), 5GB (E4B), 7GB (12B) and 15GB (26B-A4B MoE) at near-original quality, plus paths through Transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, SGLang and vLLM.
The relevance is partial: this confirms the local leg (fine-tune and serve a current multimodal model on one consumer GPU on launch day) but shows no managed hosted equivalent - the prediction's actual landing is a cloud or MLOps vendor shipping a single console that fine-tunes a small open model, wires it to a curated MCP tool catalog, and generates its own synthetic training data.
